claim: Hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine are used extensively in malaria and rheumatological conditions, and now in COVID-19 prevention and treatment.
source: Hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine are used extensively in malaria and rheumatological conditions, and now in COVID-19 prevention and treatment.
evidence: This is a statement about current medical practice that draws from established knowledge about drug usage patterns.

claim: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are potentially lethal in overdose.
source: Although generally safe they are potentially lethal in overdose.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the toxicity profile of these drugs.

claim: In-vitro data suggest that high concentrations and thus high doses are needed for COVID-19 infections.
source: In-vitro data suggest that high concentrations and thus high doses are needed for COVID-19 infections, but as yet there is no convincing evidence of clinical efficacy.
evidence: This statement references in-vitro experimental data and makes an inference about dosing requirements.

claim: There is no convincing evidence of clinical efficacy of chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19.
source: In-vitro data suggest that high concentrations and thus high doses are needed for COVID-19 infections, but as yet there is no convincing evidence of clinical efficacy.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the state of clinical evidence at the time of writing.

claim: Bayesian regression models were fitted to survival outcomes and electrocardiograph QRS durations from 302 prospectively studied French patients who had taken intentional chloroquine overdoses.
source: Bayesian regression models were fitted to survival outcomes and electrocardiograph QRS durations from 302 prospectively studied French patients who had taken intentional chloroquine overdoses, of whom 33 died (11%), and 16 healthy volunteers who took 620 mg base chloroquine single doses.
evidence: This describes the methodology and data used in the study.

claim: 33 of 302 chloroquine overdose patients died, representing 11% mortality.
source: Bayesian regression models were fitted to survival outcomes and electrocardiograph QRS durations from 302 prospectively studied French patients who had taken intentional chloroquine overdoses, of whom 33 died (11%), and 16 healthy volunteers who took 620 mg base chloroquine single doses.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient cohort data.

claim: Whole blood concentrations of 13.5 µmol/L (95% credible interval 10.1–17.7) were associated with 1% mortality.
source: Whole blood concentrations of 13.5 µmol/L (95% credible interval 10.1–17.7) were associated with 1% mortality.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian regression model fitted to the patient data.

claim: Prolongation of ventricular depolarization is concentration-dependent.
source: Prolongation of ventricular depolarization is concentration-dependent with a QRS duration >150 msec independently highly predictive of mortality in chloroquine self-poisoning.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of concentration-QRS data from the study cohorts.

claim: A QRS duration >150 msec is independently highly predictive of mortality in chloroquine self-poisoning.
source: Prolongation of ventricular depolarization is concentration-dependent with a QRS duration >150 msec independently highly predictive of mortality in chloroquine self-poisoning.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the patient data.

claim: Pharmacokinetic modeling predicts that most high dose regimens trialled in COVID-19 are unlikely to cause serious cardiovascular toxicity.
source: Pharmacokinetic modeling predicts that most high dose regimens trialled in COVID-19 are unlikely to cause serious cardiovascular toxicity.
evidence: This is a prediction based on pharmacokinetic modeling coupled with the toxicity threshold data.

claim: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are closely related 4-aminoquinoline drugs used for the treatment of malaria, amoebiasis and rheumatological conditions.
source: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are closely related 4-aminoquinoline drugs used for the treatment of malaria, amoebiasis and rheumatological conditions (World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by WHO citation.

claim: Until the late 1990s chloroquine was the drug of choice for the treatment of malaria.
source: Until the late 1990s chloroquine was the drug of choice for the treatment of malaria.
evidence: This is a historical fact about malaria treatment practices.

claim: Hundreds of tons corresponding to over 200 million doses of chloroquine were consumed annually.
source: Hundreds of tons corresponding to over 200 million doses were consumed annually.
evidence: This is a historical estimate of chloroquine usage.

claim: Chloroquine use has declined because of widespread resistance in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Since then its use has declined because of widespread resistance in Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antimalarial drug resistance.

claim: Today there is greater use of hydroxychloroquine in rheumatoid arthritis and discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus.
source: Today there is greater use of hydroxychloroquine in rheumatoid arthritis and discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus.
evidence: This is current medical practice knowledge.

claim: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are antivirals with a broad range of activities (including flaviviruses, retroviruses, and coronaviruses).
source: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are antivirals with a broad range of activities (including flaviviruses, retroviruses, and coronaviruses) (Savarino et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2020; Mégarbane and Scherrmann, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Predicted unbound concentrations of hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine in vivo with currently recommended doses are lower than the half-maximal effect concentrations reported in Vero cell cultures.
source: Their antiviral activity against SARS-CoV2 is expected to be weak as predicted unbound concentrations of hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine in vivo with currently recommended doses are lower than the half-maximal effect concentrations reported in Vero cell cultures (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on pharmacokinetic predictions and in vitro data cited from White et al., 2020.

claim: The antiviral activity of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine against SARS-CoV2 is expected to be weak.
source: Their antiviral activity against SARS-CoV2 is expected to be weak as predicted unbound concentrations of hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine in vivo with currently recommended doses are lower than the half-maximal effect concentrations reported in Vero cell cultures (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing in vivo concentrations with in vitro efficacy data.

claim: The weak antiviral activity has motivated trialling of higher loading and maintenance doses than usually given in malaria or hepatic amoebiasis.
source: This has motivated trialling of higher loading and maintenance doses than usually given in malaria or hepatic amoebiasis (World Health Organization, 2015; Conan, 1949).
evidence: This is an inference about the rationale for dose selection in COVID-19 trials.

claim: As of the 11th June 2020, 77 interventional clinical trials evaluating these drugs in both the prevention and treatment of COVID-19 were registered and recruiting participants on ClinicalTrials.gov.
source: As of the 11th June 2020, 77 interventional clinical trials evaluating these drugs in both the prevention and treatment of COVID-19 were registered and recruiting participants on ClinicalTrials.gov.
evidence: This is a factual observation from the ClinicalTrials.gov database at a specific date.

claim: The doses and durations of chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine in COVID-19 trials varied greatly.
source: The doses and durations varied greatly.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and extracted from clinical trial registrations.

claim: The high doses used by some trials have caused concern over the potential for cardiovascular toxicity.
source: The high doses used by some trials have caused concern over the potential for cardiovascular toxicity.
evidence: This reflects concerns in the medical community based on known toxicity profiles.

claim: Despite the lack of any convincing evidence of clinical benefit, these drugs are now being used extensively in COVID-19 prevention and treatment across the world.
source: Nevertheless, despite the lack of any convincing evidence of clinical benefit, these drugs are now being used extensively in COVID-19 prevention and treatment across the world.
evidence: This is an observation about clinical practice patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Patients who need hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine for the treatment of malaria and rheumatological conditions are often having difficulty obtaining them.
source: Sadly, patients who need hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine for the treatment of malaria and rheumatological conditions are often having difficulty obtaining them (Straits Times, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a news report.

claim: Borba et al. reported results from a randomised trial in Brazil of two dose regimens of chloroquine in COVID-19 treatment (CloroCovid-19 study, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04323527).
source: Borba et al. reported results from a randomised trial in Brazil of two dose regimens of chloroquine in COVID-19 treatment (CloroCovid-19 study, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04323527) (Borba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to a published clinical trial.

claim: The CloroCovid-19 trial was stopped early after recruiting only 81 patients because of cardiac toxicity and greater mortality in the higher dose group.
source: The trial was stopped early after recruiting only 81 patients because of cardiac toxicity and greater mortality in the higher dose group; two of 41 patients given the higher dose regimen developed ventricular tachycardia before death and 7 of 37 patients in this group developed electrocardiograph QTcF intervals over 500 msec compared with 4 of 36 in the lower dose group.
evidence: This is data from the Borba et al. trial.

claim: Two of 41 patients given the higher dose regimen in the CloroCovid-19 trial developed ventricular tachycardia before death.
source: The trial was stopped early after recruiting only 81 patients because of cardiac toxicity and greater mortality in the higher dose group; two of 41 patients given the higher dose regimen developed ventricular tachycardia before death and 7 of 37 patients in this group developed electrocardiograph QTcF intervals over 500 msec compared with 4 of 36 in the lower dose group.
evidence: This is specific data from the Borba et al. trial.

claim: 7 of 37 patients in the higher dose group of the CloroCovid-19 trial developed electrocardiograph QTcF intervals over 500 msec compared with 4 of 36 in the lower dose group.
source: The trial was stopped early after recruiting only 81 patients because of cardiac toxicity and greater mortality in the higher dose group; two of 41 patients given the higher dose regimen developed ventricular tachycardia before death and 7 of 37 patients in this group developed electrocardiograph QTcF intervals over 500 msec compared with 4 of 36 in the lower dose group.
evidence: This is specific data from the Borba et al. trial.

claim: The higher dose regimen in the CloroCovid-19 trial comprised 600 mg base chloroquine administered twice daily for ten days.
source: The higher dose regimen, comprising 600 mg base chloroquine administered twice daily for ten days, is substantially higher than recommended in malaria or rheumatological conditions (World Health Organization, 2015) and represents the standard malaria loading dose repeated 19 times at 12 hr intervals.
evidence: This is a description of the trial protocol from Borba et al.

claim: The higher dose regimen in the CloroCovid-19 trial is substantially higher than recommended in malaria or rheumatological conditions.
source: The higher dose regimen, comprising 600 mg base chloroquine administered twice daily for ten days, is substantially higher than recommended in malaria or rheumatological conditions (World Health Organization, 2015) and represents the standard malaria loading dose repeated 19 times at 12 hr intervals.
evidence: This is a comparison with established treatment guidelines.

claim: The higher dose regimen in the CloroCovid-19 trial represents the standard malaria loading dose repeated 19 times at 12 hr intervals.
source: The higher dose regimen, comprising 600 mg base chloroquine administered twice daily for ten days, is substantially higher than recommended in malaria or rheumatological conditions (World Health Organization, 2015) and represents the standard malaria loading dose repeated 19 times at 12 hr intervals.
evidence: This is a calculation based on comparing the trial dose to standard malaria treatment.

claim: Chloroquine is dangerous in overdose and has been used extensively for suicide.
source: Chloroquine is dangerous in overdose and has been used extensively for suicide.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about chloroquine toxicity.

claim: High concentrations of chloroquine cause hypotension, arrhythmias, coma, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and fatal cardiac arrest.
source: High concentrations of chloroquine cause hypotension, arrhythmias, coma, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and fatal cardiac arrest (Riou et al., 1988; Clemessy et al., 1995; Clemessy et al., 1996; Mégarbane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of chloroquine poisoning.

claim: In Zimbabwe the mortality of chloroquine in overdose was approximately six times higher than for other drugs.
source: In Zimbabwe the mortality of chloroquine in overdose was approximately six times higher than for other drugs (Ball et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study in Zimbabwe.

claim: In France in the early 1980s there was a suicide epidemic following the publication of a book entitled Suicide: mode d'emploi (Suicide: a how-to guide).
source: In France in the early 1980s there was a suicide epidemic (Riou et al., 1988; Clemessy et al., 1995; Clemessy et al., 1996; Mégarbane et al., 2010 ) following the publication of a book entitled Suicide: mode d'emploi (Suicide: a how-to guide) (Guillon and Le Bonniec, 1982).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by multiple citations.

claim: Outcome in chloroquine self-poisoning depends on the dose ingested, the delay in reaching hospital and the quality of intensive care support.
source: Outcome in chloroquine self-poisoning depends on the dose ingested, the delay in reaching hospital and the quality of intensive care support.
evidence: This is an inference from the clinical experience and data from the French cohorts.

claim: Individual patient whole blood chloroquine + desethylchloroquine concentrations and outcomes were pooled from three large prospectively studied French hospital self-poisoning cohorts (n = 302).
source: We pooled individual patient whole blood chloroquine + desethylchloroquine concentrations and outcomes from three large prospectively studied hospital self-poisoning cohorts (n = 302, Figure 2, top panel) (Riou et al., 1988; Clemessy et al., 1995; Clemessy et al., 1996; Mégarbane et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the analysis.

claim: All the patients included in this analysis were treated in the same hospital in Paris and all had whole blood concentrations measured on admission.
source: All the patients included in this analysis were treated in the same hospital in Paris and all had whole blood concentrations measured on admission.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the patient cohort.

claim: The overall mortality was 11% (33 of 302).
source: The overall mortality was 11% (33 of 302).
evidence: This is a direct calculation from the patient data.

claim: The distribution of differences on the log scale between admission whole blood concentrations and peak concentrations in patients who peaked after hospital admission was used to estimate a correction term for all other patients.
source: The distribution of differences on the log scale between admission whole blood concentrations and peak concentrations in patients who peaked after hospital admission was used to estimate a correction term for all other patients.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the analysis.

claim: Bayesian logistic regression was used to estimate the relationship between mortality and inferred whole blood peak chloroquine concentrations.
source: Bayesian logistic regression was used to estimate the relationship between mortality and inferred whole blood peak chloroquine concentrations (Figure 2, bottom panel) specifically adjusted for the desethyl metabolite levels and for the non-observed peak concentrations in 241 (80%) of the patients.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used.

claim: The model adjusted for the desethyl metabolite levels and for the non-observed peak concentrations in 241 (80%) of the patients.
source: Bayesian logistic regression was used to estimate the relationship between mortality and inferred whole blood peak chloroquine concentrations (Figure 2, bottom panel) specifically adjusted for the desethyl metabolite levels and for the non-observed peak concentrations in 241 (80%) of the patients.
evidence: This describes adjustments made in the statistical model.

claim: The model also adjusted for differences in treatment received between cohorts.
source: The model also adjusted for differences in treatment received between cohorts.
evidence: This describes another adjustment made in the statistical model.

claim: 1% is the lowest mortality for which a reliable estimate can be derived from these data.
source: 1% is the lowest mortality for which a reliable estimate can be derived from these data.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical limitations of the analysis.

claim: The 1% threshold value was used to evaluate the risk of fatal toxicity in chloroquine treatment regimens under evaluation in COVID-19.
source: The 1% threshold value was then used to evaluate the risk of fatal toxicity in chloroquine treatment regimens under evaluation in COVID-19.
evidence: This describes how the threshold was applied to COVID-19 treatment regimens.

claim: Two pharmacokinetic models were used to predict peak chloroquine concentrations for six chloroquine regimens.
source: We used two pharmacokinetic models to predict peak chloroquine concentrations for six chloroquine regimens.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used.

claim: Five of the simulated regimens are potential COVID treatment regimens, and one is the standard malaria treatment regimen.
source: Five of the simulated regimens are potential COVID treatment regimens, and one is the standard malaria treatment regimen.
evidence: This describes the regimens that were simulated.

claim: The pharmacokinetic model estimated from whole blood concentrations predicted a slightly wider range of values for maximum chloroquine concentrations (Cmax) than the plasma-based model.
source: The pharmacokinetic model estimated from whole blood concentrations (Höglund et al., 2016) predicted a slightly wider range of values for maximum chloroquine concentrations (Cmax) than the plasma-based model (Appendix 3 shows the predicted Cmax distributions for both models in a 70 kg adult).
evidence: This is a comparison of two pharmacokinetic models.

claim: Assuming a whole blood to plasma concentration ratio of 4, the whole blood-based model and the plasma-based model predicted approximately identical median Cmax values.
source: Assuming a whole blood to plasma concentration ratio of 4, the whole blood-based model and the plasma-based model predicted approximately identical median Cmax values.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two pharmacokinetic models.

claim: The whole blood pharmacokinetic model provides higher estimates for fatal toxicity because it predicts a larger variance for the Cmax distribution and hence more extreme outliers.
source: Thus, the whole blood pharmacokinetic model provides higher estimates for fatal toxicity because it predicts a larger variance for the Cmax distribution and hence more extreme outliers.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the model differences.

claim: The median Cmax following a chloroquine dose of 600 mg base equivalent given twice daily for ten days to a 70 kg adult is 10.7 µmol/L.
source: Based on the whole blood model, the median Cmax following a chloroquine dose of 600 mg base equivalent given twice daily for ten days to a 70 kg adult is 10.7 µmol/L (Figure 3, panel A).
evidence: This is a prediction from the pharmacokinetic model.

claim: The median Cmax for the 600 mg twice daily regimen is more than three times higher than the median Cmax for the chloroquine malaria treatment regimen at the same body weight.
source: This is more than three times higher than the median Cmax for the chloroquine malaria treatment regimen at the same body weight.
evidence: This is a comparison of pharmacokinetic predictions between regimens.

claim: Approximately 60% of 70 kg adults continuing to receive the twice daily 600 mg dose have blood concentrations which rise into the 'danger zone' defined as whole blood concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
source: Approximately 60% of 70 kg adults continuing to receive the twice daily 600 mg dose have blood concentrations which rise into the 'danger zone' defined as whole blood concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a prediction from the pharmacokinetic model combined with the toxicity threshold.

claim: Only two in a thousand 70 kg adults receiving the twice daily 310 mg base maintenance dose for ten days would reach concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
source: In comparison, only two in a thousand 70 kg adults receiving the twice daily 310 mg base maintenance dose (as given in the SOLIDARITY and RECOVERY trials) for ten days would reach concentrations above 10 µmol/L (approximately the lower bound for the 1% mortality threshold).
evidence: This is a prediction from the pharmacokinetic model.

claim: Fewer than one per thousand receiving the twice daily 310 mg dose would have peak concentrations above the 1% mortality threshold.
source: Taking into account the uncertainty around this threshold value, the model estimates that fewer than one per thousand receiving the twice daily 310 mg dose would have peak concentrations above the 1% mortality threshold (Figure 3, panel B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the coupled pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model.

claim: Body weight is an important determinant of exposure if doses are not adjusted for weight.
source: Clearly body weight is an important determinant of exposure if doses are not adjusted for weight, as is common with oral administration (chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine tablets usually contain 155 mg base).
evidence: This is an inference from pharmacokinetic principles and the modeling results.

claim: At most, two in a thousand 40 kg adults receiving the 3 day malaria treatment regimen without weight adjustment are predicted to reach peak concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
source: At most, two in a thousand 40 kg adults receiving the 3 day malaria treatment regimen without weight adjustment (i.e. an unusually high mg/kg dose) are predicted to reach peak concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a prediction from the pharmacokinetic model for a specific scenario.

claim: Administering 600 mg base equivalent of chloroquine phosphate twice daily for ten days is predicted to result in absolute mean fatality ratios ranging between 0.05% (90 kg, 95% credible interval (C.I.), 0% to 0.3%) and 3.5% (40 kg, 95% C.I. 1.0% to 8.0%).
source: Administering 600 mg base equivalent of chloroquine phosphate twice daily for ten days as in the CloroCovid-19 trial is predicted to result in absolute mean fatality ratios ranging between 0.05% (90 kg, 95% credible interval (C.I.), 0% to 0.3%) and 3.5% (40 kg, 95% C.I. 1.0% to 8.0%), Figure 3, panel C.
evidence: This is a prediction from the coupled pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model.

claim: Only the flat dosing regimens are predicted to result in fatality ratios greater than one per thousand, and then only for weights less than 55 kg.
source: In comparison, only the flat dosing regimens are predicted to result in fatality ratios greater than one per thousand, and then only for weights less than 55 kg: for a 40 kg adult the 10 day SOLIDARITY regimen could result in 0.2% mortality (95% CI, 0 to 0.8).
evidence: This is a prediction from the coupled pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model.

claim: For a 40 kg adult the 10 day SOLIDARITY regimen could result in 0.2% mortality (95% CI, 0 to 0.8).
source: In comparison, only the flat dosing regimens are predicted to result in fatality ratios greater than one per thousand, and then only for weights less than 55 kg: for a 40 kg adult the 10 day SOLIDARITY regimen could result in 0.2% mortality (95% CI, 0 to 0.8).
evidence: This is a specific prediction from the model for a particular weight and regimen.

claim: The 10 day flat regimen of 500 mg chloroquine phosphate salt (310 mg base equivalent) twice daily was recommended by the Health Commission of Guangdong Province for adults weighing more than 50 kg.
source: The 10 day flat regimen (without a loading dose) of 500 mg chloroquine phosphate salt (310 mg base equivalent) twice daily was recommended by the Health Commission of Guangdong Province for adults weighing more than 50 kg (Multicenter collaboration group of Department of Science and Technology of Guangdong Province and Health Commission of Guangdong Province for chloroquine in the treatment of novel coronavirus pneumonia, 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to treatment guidelines from Guangdong Province.

claim: The Guangdong Province regimen is not predicted to incur a significant risk of cardiotoxicity.
source: This is not predicted to incur a significant risk of cardiotoxicity.
evidence: This is a prediction from the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model.

claim: The model predictions support the body weight threshold of 50 kg for dose reduction recommended by Guangdong Province.
source: Overall the model predictions support this body weight threshold for dose reduction.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Individual electrocardiograph QRS intervals and chloroquine concentration data were pooled from 16 healthy volunteers and 290 self-poisoning patients.
source: We pooled individual electrocardiograph QRS intervals and chloroquine concentration data from 16 healthy volunteers (Pukrittayakamee et al., 2014, for each individual the QRS interval was measured twice at rest and 12 times in presence of detectable plasma chloroquine concentrations after a single 620 mg base oral dose of chloroquine phosphate), and 290 self-poisoning patients (no QRS data from Riou et al., and one missing QRS measurement from the Clemessy cohort), Figure 4.
evidence: This describes the data sources for the QRS analysis.

claim: A whole blood chloroquine concentration of 3 µmol/L is associated with a slight QRS prolongation of 6.7 msec (95% credible interval, 5.5–7.8).
source: A whole blood chloroquine concentration of 3 µmol/L (usually observed in malaria treatment) is associated with a slight QRS prolongation of 6.7 msec (95% credible interval, 5.5–7.8).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian regression model fitted to the QRS data.

claim: Clinically significant intraventricular conduction delay (QRS prolongation), resulting in durations greater than 150 msec, was strongly associated with observed chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
source: Clinically significant intraventricular conduction delay (QRS prolongation), resulting in durations greater than 150 msec, was strongly associated with observed chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the concentration-QRS data.

claim: In self-poisoning, 1 out of 108 patients with admission whole blood concentrations less than 10 µmol/L had a QRS interval longer than 150 msec.
source: In self-poisoning, 1 out of 108 patients with admission whole blood concentrations less than 10 µmol/L had a QRS interval longer than 150 msec (this accounts for the bias term estimated in the Clemessy cohort).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: QRS durations longer than 150 msec were recorded in 36 out of 182 (20%) of the patients with whole blood concentrations greater than 10 µmol/L.
source: In comparison, QRS durations longer than 150 msec were recorded in 36 out of 182 (20%) of the patients with whole blood concentrations greater than 10 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the patient data.

claim: Chloroquine is dangerous in overdose.
source: Chloroquine is dangerous in overdose.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by the study data.

claim: The risk of death is proportional to drug exposure.
source: The risk of death is proportional to drug exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the concentration-mortality analysis.

claim: Mortality rises steeply at whole blood chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
source: Mortality rises steeply at whole blood chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a finding from the concentration-mortality model.

claim: Whole blood chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L correspond very approximately to a plasma concentration of 3 µmol/L.
source: This corresponds very approximately to a plasma concentration of 3 µmol/L, and a combined chloroquine and desethylchloroquine concentration (as in a spectrophotometric assay) of 14 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a conversion based on known blood-to-plasma ratios.

claim: Whole blood chloroquine concentrations above 10 µmol/L correspond to a combined chloroquine and desethylchloroquine concentration of 14 µmol/L.
source: This corresponds very approximately to a plasma concentration of 3 µmol/L, and a combined chloroquine and desethylchloroquine concentration (as in a spectrophotometric assay) of 14 µmol/L.
evidence: This is a conversion accounting for the metabolite contribution.

claim: The electrocardiograph is a valuable indicator of toxicity as potentially lethal levels are associated with significant QRS complex widening.
source: Importantly the electrocardiograph is a valuable indicator of toxicity as potentially lethal levels are associated with significant QRS complex widening.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the concentration-QRS analysis.

claim: A QRS duration of less than 100 msec makes lethal toxicity very unlikely.
source: A QRS duration of less than 100 msec makes lethal toxicity very unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference from the concentration-QRS data and mortality data.

claim: When using high-dose treatments weight adjusted dosing is important to avoid toxicity.
source: When using high-dose treatments weight adjusted dosing is important to avoid toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pharmacokinetic modeling showing weight-dependent exposure.

claim: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are already being used extensively, and often in high doses, to prevent and treat COVID-19 despite the current lack of convincing evidence of benefit.
source: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are already being used extensively, and often in high doses, to prevent and treat COVID-19 despite the current lack of convincing evidence of benefit.
evidence: This is an observation about clinical practice during the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Use of these drugs has become extremely politicised.
source: Use of these drugs has become extremely politicised.
evidence: This is an observation about the social and political context of drug use during COVID-19.

claim: The first large randomised trial (RECOVERY) in the treatment of hospitalised COVID-19 patients strongly suggests that hydroxychloroquine does not benefit hospitalised patients.
source: The first large randomised trial in the treatment of hospitalised patients has just reported (RECOVERY, NCT04381936: press release only at the time of writing, results are not yet peer reviewed). This result strongly suggests that hydroxychloroquine (and also lopinavir-ritonavir) does not benefit hospitalised patients.
evidence: This is based on preliminary results from the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The RECOVERY trial results strongly suggest that lopinavir-ritonavir does not benefit hospitalised COVID-19 patients.
source: The first large randomised trial in the treatment of hospitalised patients has just reported (RECOVERY, NCT04381936: press release only at the time of writing, results are not yet peer reviewed). This result strongly suggests that hydroxychloroquine (and also lopinavir-ritonavir) does not benefit hospitalised patients.
evidence: This is based on preliminary results from the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The preliminary results of the RECOVERY trial show that dexamethasone has a major life saving benefit in patients receiving oxygen or being ventilated.
source: The preliminary results of the same trial show that dexamethasone has a major life saving benefit in patients receiving oxygen or being ventilated.
evidence: This is based on preliminary results from the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The RECOVERY trial results support a paradigm of early benefit from an effective antiviral and late benefit from an anti-inflammatory drug.
source: This supports a paradigm of early benefit from an effective antiviral and late benefit from an anti-inflammatory drug.
evidence: This is an inference from the RECOVERY trial results.

claim: There remains a potential role for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine in prevention and early treatment of COVID-19.
source: Thus there remains a potential role for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine in prevention and early treatment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of benefit in hospitalized patients but potential for benefit earlier in disease.

claim: A recent high profile claim of increased mortality and high rates of ventricular arrhythmia in a very large observational data set was almost certainly fabricated.
source: Confusion over the risks associated with chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine has been compounded by a recent high profile claim of increased mortality and high rates of ventricular arrhythmia in a very large observational data set. This data set was almost certainly fabricated (and the paper was subsequently retracted, Mehra et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to a retracted paper and is based on the retraction.

claim: The fabricated paper was subsequently retracted.
source: Confusion over the risks associated with chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine has been compounded by a recent high profile claim of increased mortality and high rates of ventricular arrhythmia in a very large observational data set. This data set was almost certainly fabricated (and the paper was subsequently retracted, Mehra et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about a paper retraction.

claim: Over-reactions by some regulatory agencies, unjustified extrapolations of risk from QT measurements, failure to distinguish the effects of the drugs given alone from the combination with azithromycin, and misunderstanding of their clinical pharmacology have conspired to reduce confidence in these drugs and jeopardise the very trials needed to characterise risks and benefits in the prevention and treatment of COVID-19.
source: Unfortunately over-reactions by some regulatory agencies, unjustified extrapolations of risk from QT measurements, failure to distinguish the effects of the drugs given alone from the combination with azithromycin, and misunderstanding of their clinical pharmacology have conspired to reduce confidence in these drugs and jeopardise the very trials needed to characterise risks and benefits in the prevention and treatment of COVID-19 (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an opinion/assessment of the regulatory and research environment, supported by a citation.

claim: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine have unusual pharmacokinetic properties with very large total apparent volumes of distribution (Vd) and very slow terminal elimination rates.
source: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine have unusual pharmacokinetic properties with very large total apparent volumes of distribution (Vd) (chloroquine > hydroxychloroquine) and very slow terminal elimination rates (terminal half-lives exceed one month) which cannot be measured accurately.
evidence: This is established pharmacokinetic knowledge about these drugs.

claim: Chloroquine has a larger volume of distribution than hydroxychloroquine.
source: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine have unusual pharmacokinetic properties with very large total apparent volumes of distribution (Vd) (chloroquine > hydroxychloroquine) and very slow terminal elimination rates (terminal half-lives exceed one month) which cannot be measured accurately.
evidence: This is established pharmacokinetic knowledge.

claim: Terminal half-lives of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine exceed one month.
